name: tokio-postgres (async PostgreSQL driver)
baseline: sqlx 0.8 PostgreSQL driver (query_as! macro and query + FromRow)
verdict_reason: tokio-postgres loads large result sets 1.5x faster than sqlx's macro path and 1.9x faster than its FromRow path at 10,000 rows. On one-row queries in the same suite it was 1.56x slower than sqlx, so the win depends on result size.
tier_reason: Public suite run nightly in CI by the Diesel project, independent of both drivers, with toolchain and RUSTFLAGS stated.
claimed_speedup: Trivial select, median: 10000 rows 2,190.77 us vs 3,347.92 us (query_as!) and 4,133.86 us (FromRow), 1.53x and 1.89x; 1 row 53.45 us vs 34.32 us (sqlx faster). User report fetching 12096001 rows: 9386ms vs 29830ms for sqlx query_as (ratios derived from page data).
workload: Diesel benchmark 'trivial query' against a local PostgreSQL 18: SELECT returning 1 to 10,000 user rows into structs; a separate user report fetched 12 million 6-column rows.
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner (shared VM, CPU not recorded)
os: Ubuntu (GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest image), PostgreSQL 18 on localhost
toolchain: rustc stable via rustup on the run date, RUSTFLAGS=-C target-cpu=native, cargo bench
one_liner: Async PostgreSQL driver; 1.5x to 1.9x faster than sqlx on 10,000-row results, slower on one-row queries in the same suite.
how_it_is_fast: tokio-postgres decodes rows lazily from the binary protocol buffer and supports pipelining several queries on one connection. sqlx adds its own row and type-mapping layer, which costs more as the row count grows.
use_it_when: Endpoints that return thousands of rows per query
You can pipeline independent queries, which sqlx does not support
skip_it_when: Mostly single-row lookups, where sqlx was faster in this suite
You want compile-time checked SQL (sqlx macros) or a query builder (Diesel)
caveats: Shared CI VM; numbers change run to run (this record uses the 2026-10-27 run)
Suite pins sqlx 0.8; sqlx 0.9 (May 2026) is not measured
The one-row result may reflect per-iteration runtime overhead in the harness: the synchronous postgres crate, which wraps tokio-postgres, took 30.22 us
The 12M-row report ran tokio-postgres first, so database caching may have favored the second library less than it seems
tradeoffs: No connection pool, migrations or compile-time query checks built in
Row-to-struct mapping is manual or needs a helper crate

evidence.quote: This is with tokio-postgres running the query first, sqlx second, so the db might cache something already for sqlx?
Query Pipelining is supported by diesel-async and tokio-postgres
Notably sqlx and sea-orm do not support this feature.
